passage: Jeevan had just got his first debit card, linked to the account where his scholarship money came. His aunt Rashmi, who ran a small grocery in their town, helped him set up a payment app. "Rule one," she said, "never share your PIN or OTP. Not even with me." A week later, a man called, saying he was from the bank. "Your card will be blocked. Just tell me the OTP you receive." Jeevan's heart jumped. Then he remembered. "I'll go to the branch," he said and hung up. His hands were shaking. Rashmi Maasi took him to the branch, where the manager said it was a common fraud. That evening she also helped him write a simple budget in a notebook: fees, bus, books, savings.

qa.q: What did the caller ask Jeevan to tell him?
qa.a: He asked for the OTP Jeevan received.

qa.q: Why were Jeevan's hands shaking after he hung up?
qa.a: He had been scared the card would be blocked and realised how close he came to a fraud, so the fear and relief were still in his body.

qa.q: What was wise about Jeevan's response to the caller?
qa.a: He refused to share the OTP and chose to go to the branch in person, checking with a real source instead of the caller.

qa.q: How might Rashmi Maasi feel after the call?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and proud that her rule stuck, and it gave her a chance to also teach him budgeting.

grounding: It shows a teen using a card and payment app safely, spotting a fraud call and starting a simple budget.

passage: Bao got his first bank card at sixteen in Hanoi and used it to buy snacks, games, and bus fares. By the end of the month, the money from his part-time job at his uncle's shop was almost gone. He couldn't remember where it went. His friend Paulo, whose family had moved from Brazil, showed him a notebook. "I write everything down. Every coin." Bao laughed, but that evening he checked his account. Twenty small payments for games he had forgotten. His face went hot. He made a simple table: needs, wants, savings. He also set a spending alert. The next month, he still bought one game, but he knew exactly how much was left.

qa.q: How many small payments for games did Bao find?
qa.a: He found twenty small payments for games.

qa.q: Why did Bao's face go hot when he checked his account?
qa.a: He was embarrassed to see how many forgotten game payments had eaten up his earnings.

qa.q: What made Bao's new system work?
qa.a: Sorting spending into needs, wants and savings and setting an alert helped him see his money clearly without banning all fun.

qa.q: How might Paulo feel seeing Bao adopt Paulo's idea?
qa.a: Paulo might feel pleased that the notebook habit from home helped a friend. 👍

grounding: It shows a teen tracking small card payments and starting a simple budget.

passage: In the Class 11 commerce lab, the teacher ran a mock exercise: each student got a pretend wallet of money for a month and a set of messages to handle. Omkar opened one: "Congratulations! You've won a phone. Pay a small fee to claim." He almost clicked "pay." Bhavna, beside him, pointed at the screen. "Why would a prize need a fee?" Omkar frowned and marked it as fraud. The next message asked him to scan a QR code to receive money. Bhavna said, "Scanning is for paying, not receiving." By the end, Omkar had spotted four frauds and made a budget that left some savings. He was surprised at how easy the tricks were to miss. "I'm showing this to my dad," he said.

qa.q: What did the first message say Omkar had won?
qa.a: It said he had won a phone.

qa.q: Why was Omkar surprised by the end of the exercise?
qa.a: He realised how easily he almost fell for the tricks, which showed him fraud can look convincing.

qa.q: Why was the mock exercise a good teaching method?
qa.a: It let students practise spotting fraud and budgeting without real money at risk, so mistakes became lessons.

qa.q: How might Omkar's dad react when Omkar shows him the exercise?
qa.a: He might be surprised and thankful, and it could make them both more careful with their own payments.

grounding: It shows teens in a school lab practising spotting payment fraud and making a simple budget.

passage:
Hi Neelam,
Since you just got your first UPI account, here's a story so you don't make my mistake, almost.
Last week a man called saying he was from a delivery company and wanted to refund me ₹499. He sent a QR code and said, 'Scan and enter your PIN to receive.' I was about to do it! Then I remembered Papa saying you NEVER need your PIN to receive money. Only to pay. I cut the call and my hands were shaking. I reported the number on the helpline.
Also, I've started a notebook budget: pocket money in, what I spend out. Turns out half went on canteen samosas. So now I save a little first.
Stay sharp,
Gargi didi

qa.q: What did the caller ask Gargi to do?
qa.a: Scan a QR code and enter her PIN to 'receive' a refund of ₹499.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel after she cut the call?
qa.a: She felt shaken, with trembling hands, because she had almost fallen for it.

qa.q: What rule saved Gargi from the scam?
qa.a: That you never need your PIN to receive money, only to pay.

qa.q: How might Neelam benefit from Gargi admitting she nearly fell for it?
qa.a: Hearing an honest near-miss from Gargi didi makes the warning feel real and less preachy.

grounding: A teen writes about spotting a digital payment fraud and keeping a simple budget.

passage: So Sumit, you asked why I stopped lending money to people online. Listen. Last month, someone in a gaming group said he'd pay me double if I lent him five hundred for a tournament entry. He even sent a screenshot of 'payment sent' first. I checked my account. Nothing had come. The screenshot was fake. Then he got angry, saying, 'Send now, bro, it's urgent!' The pressure was the giveaway. I blocked him and told my mother. We reported the profile. After that I sat down and made a simple budget. Pocket money in, expenses out, and a small amount saved. Turns out I was spending most of it on game upgrades. I'm Mridul, sixteen, and now I check before I trust.

qa.q: What did the stranger send Mridul first?
qa.a: A screenshot saying 'payment sent'.

qa.q: Why did Mridul become suspicious of the stranger?
qa.a: Mridul's account showed no money, and the stranger's urgent pressure felt like a warning sign.

qa.q: What did Mridul do after spotting the fraud?
qa.a: Mridul blocked the stranger, told their mother, reported the profile and started a simple budget.

qa.q: How might Sumit use Mridul's story?
qa.a: Sumit could learn to check the account before trusting screenshots and to treat urgent pressure as a red flag.

grounding: A teen recounts spotting fraud in online money requests and starting a simple budget.

passage:
I'm Tanuja, Reena's aunt. Last week, while Reena, seventeen, was helping me cook, her phone rang.
“Hello, I'm calling from your bank. Your account will be blocked. Tell me the OTP we just sent.”
Reena's face tightened. “I'll call my bank directly from the number on my card,” she said, and hung up.
I asked how she knew. She shrugged. “Banks never ask for OTPs. Our teacher told us.”
Later she showed me her small notebook. Every rupee from her pocket money and tuition income was written down: phone recharge, bus pass, a birthday gift. At the bottom she'd written what was left and circled it.
I don't remember being that careful at her age.

qa.q: What did the caller ask Reena for?
qa.a: The OTP they just sent.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when she heard the caller's request?
qa.a: She felt suspicious and alert, her face tightening.

qa.q: What safe steps did Reena take with money?
qa.a: She refused to share the OTP, planned to call the bank directly, and kept a notebook of her spending.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Reena's carefulness?
qa.a: Tanuja is impressed, feeling Reena is more careful than she was at that age.

grounding: An aunt observes a seventeen-year-old spot a phone fraud and keep a simple budget.

passage:
First week of term: Gurpreet, seventeen, got his first debit card and a payment app. By Friday, half his month's allowance had gone on canteen snacks and late-night food orders. He hadn't noticed until the balance message came.
Two weeks later: His friend Lokesh got a message from a stranger: Scan this QR code to receive ₹2,000 for your old phone. Lokesh was about to scan. Gurpreet stopped him. “You scan to pay, not to receive. That's a trick.” They blocked the number.
End of month: Gurpreet sat down with his mother and made a simple list on paper: bus, food, phone, savings. He decided to check his balance every Sunday. Lokesh copied it.

qa.q: What did the stranger's message tell Lokesh to do?
qa.a: To scan a QR code to receive ₹2,000 for his old phone.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when he saw his balance message in the first week?
qa.a: He felt shocked and uneasy, realising how much he had spent without noticing.

qa.q: What steps helped Gurpreet manage money more safely?
qa.a: Spotting the QR scam, blocking the number, and making a simple budget with his mother.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt when Gurpreet stopped him?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed but relieved that he didn't lose money.

grounding: Over a month a seventeen-year-old learns to budget and spot a digital payment scam.

passage:
Payal, you think these phone frauds only catch old people? Let your Bidisha Pishi tell you.
When I was a clerk at the bank in Kolkata, a young man came in one morning, maybe nineteen, white in the face. He'd got a call saying he'd won a scholarship. To release it, he just had to share the code on his phone. He did. His savings from tuition teaching were gone in a minute.
He kept saying, “It sounded so real.”
That same week, an old lady came to my counter wanting to transfer money to a “nephew” she'd never met. I asked her to wait and call her daughter first. She did. It was a fraud.
No bank or scholarship will ever ask for your code, Payal. When in doubt, stop and ask someone you trust.

qa.q: What did the young man think he had won?
qa.a: A scholarship.

qa.q: How did the young man feel after losing his savings?
qa.a: He felt shocked and devastated, white in the face.

qa.q: What choice inside the story stopped a fraud?
qa.a: Bidisha asking the old lady to wait and call her daughter before transferring the money.

qa.q: How might the old lady have felt after calling her daughter?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved and grateful that Bidisha stopped her in time.

grounding: An aunt tells her niece about digital payment frauds she saw at the bank and how to avoid them.

passage:
Hafsa was selling her old cycle online. A buyer messaged: "I'll pay now. Just scan this QR code to receive the money."
She was in a rush; her bus was due and the buyer kept messaging: "Quick, or I'll buy another one."
Hafsa opened the scanner. Then her friend Gargi grabbed her arm. "Wait. You never scan to receive money. Scanning is for paying."
Hafsa looked. The screen said "Pay Rs 4,500". Her heart jumped.
"That would've taken money from my account!"
She blocked the buyer, took a screenshot and reported it on the cyber crime helpline, 1930, with her father that evening. Then she added a note in her phone: "Receiving money = no scan, no PIN."

qa.q: What did the screen say when Hafsa opened the scanner?
What was Hafsa feeling when her heart jumped?
qa.a: Hafsa felt shocked and scared, realising she almost lost money.

qa.q: What steps did Hafsa take after spotting the scam?
qa.a: She blocked the buyer, took a screenshot, and reported it with her father on the cyber crime helpline.

qa.q: How does Gargi see the QR code request?
qa.a: Gargi sees it as a scam because scanning is for paying, not receiving.

grounding: Under time pressure a teen nearly falls for a QR code scam, spots it and reports it.

passage:
Every month Hansa got her pocket money into her own bank account, linked to her phone. And every month, by the 20th, it was gone.
"Where does it go?" asked her father, Santosh.
Hansa shrugged. "Snacks? Stuff?"
So Santosh suggested she track it. For one month, Hansa wrote every payment in a notes app: canteen, auto, a phone cover, gifts.
At the end she was shocked. Almost half went on canteen snacks and small online orders she didn't even remember.
She made three columns: needs, wants, saving. She didn't stop the snacks, but she cut the small orders. Next month, she still had some left on the 30th.
She showed Santosh the notes. He grinned. "You're better at this than me."

qa.q: By which date was Hansa's pocket money usually gone?
qa.a: By the 20th.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she saw where the money went?
qa.a: Hansa felt shocked and a little embarrassed at how much went on things she didn't remember.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that helped her keep track?
qa.a: She wrote down every payment for a month, then sorted spending into needs, wants and saving.

qa.q: How does Santosh see Hansa's tracking?
qa.a: Santosh is proud and impressed, even joking she's better at it than him.

grounding: A teen tracks her digital payments to understand her spending and make a simple budget.

passage:
"Aditi, my payment app is showing an error. I called customer care," said Deepak, her brother, holding his phone.
"Where did you get the number?"
"Online. The first search result."
Aditi frowned. "What did they say?"
"They said to share the OTP so they can fix it."
"Don't! Real companies never ask for OTPs."
"But he sounded so official."
"That's the trick. Hang up."
Deepak hung up, hands trembling. "I almost told him."
Aditi opened the official app and found the real help section. "Always use the app itself, not a search result."
They told their mother that evening and reported the number to the cyber crime helpline together.

qa.q: Where did Deepak find the customer care number?
qa.a: The first search result online.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when his hands were trembling?
qa.a: Deepak felt shaken and scared, realising how close he came to sharing the OTP.

qa.q: What did Aditi teach Deepak about getting help?
qa.a: Never share an OTP, and use the official app's help section instead of a search result.

qa.q: How does Aditi see the caller?
qa.a: Aditi sees the official-sounding voice as part of the scam, not a sign of a real company.

grounding: A teen stops her brother from sharing an OTP with fake customer care and they report it.

passage:
Last month I got a call from someone saying he was from a shopping site. He said I'd been charged twice for my headphones and he'd refund it. "I'm sending a request on UPI. Just accept and enter your PIN to receive the money."
I actually had my thumb on the screen. Then I remembered what my friend Jomon had shown me after his sister nearly got cheated: you never need a PIN to receive money. A PIN is only for sending.
I said I'd call back and hung up. My hands were shaking. I showed the request to my father. He checked with the bank's official number, which said they'd never call like that, and he reported the number.
I'm Kiran, and now I read every UPI screen twice, especially the word "pay".

qa.q: What did the caller say he would do?
qa.a: He said he'd refund the double charge by sending a request on UPI.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after hanging up?
qa.a: Kiran felt shaken and scared, with shaking hands, realising how close it had been.

qa.q: Why was showing the request to Kiran's father the right step?
qa.a: He could verify with the bank's official number and report the fraud, rather than Kiran handling it alone.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel if he learned his tip had helped?
qa.a: Jomon would probably feel glad and proud that his sister's close call protected his friend.

grounding: Shows a teen spotting a UPI refund scam and involving a parent to verify and report it.

passage:
Class 9 life-skills note. Yogesh, maths teacher.
This month the class tracked their own pocket money for three weeks, then we discussed patterns. I asked them not to share amounts, only what they noticed.
Aadhya's notebook was the most honest. She'd written every item: bus, a pen, snacks. When she added it up, snacks from the school gate were more than everything else together. She was surprised and a little embarrassed. "They're so small each time," she said.
She decided on her own to carry fruit twice a week and to keep a simple table: what came in, what went out, what was left. She also asked whether she should keep her money in the family's bank account. I told her that's a question for her parents, and a bank official if they want.
I'll ask the class to reflect again at the end of term.

qa.q: What was Aadhya surprised to find she spent most on?
qa.a: Snacks from the school gate were more than everything else together.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when she added up her snacks?
qa.a: Aadhya felt surprised and a little embarrassed, since each purchase had seemed so small.

qa.q: What did Yogesh handle wisely when Aadhya asked about a bank account?
qa.a: He pointed her to her parents and a bank official instead of giving personal money advice himself.

qa.q: How might Aadhya's classmates see her findings?
qa.a: They might feel curious to check their own small spends, since hers surprised her so much.

grounding: Illustrates a teen keeping a simple budget and noticing spending patterns, with a teacher guiding without personal money rules.

passage:
Saturday
Diary, Jyoti here. Got my first debit card today! Mummy (Manjula, but I'll never call her that) took me to the bank and then to the ATM.
Things she made me do:
Cover the keypad with my hand when typing the PIN, even though nobody was there.
Never tell anyone the PIN or OTP, not even her, not even "someone from the bank" on the phone.
Check the SMS after every payment.
At the canteen I paid with UPI and the amount on the screen said 250 instead of 25. My heart jumped. I cancelled and asked the uncle to type it again. He said sorry, he'd hit an extra zero.
Mummy said that's exactly why you look before you press. Also started a notebook: in, out, left. So far: very little left.

qa.q: What amount did the canteen screen show instead of 25?
qa.a: It said 250 instead of 25.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel on seeing the wrong amount?
qa.a: Jyoti felt a jolt of alarm, heart jumping, before calmly cancelling it.

qa.q: Which of Jyoti's habits helped at the canteen, and why?
qa.a: Looking before pressing helped, because it caught the extra zero before the payment went through.

qa.q: How might the canteen uncle have felt when Jyoti asked him to re-type?
qa.a: He was probably a little embarrassed but grateful the mistake was caught before it caused trouble.

grounding: Shows a teen learning card and UPI safety habits and starting a simple budget.
